title: The Integrity of the Personality
author: Anthony Storr
one_line_takeaway: Psychological health is not conformity to an external standard but the realization and integration of one's own unique, given nature—including its darker and more antisocial elements.
synopsis:
Anthony Storr's first book, written early in his career as a psychotherapist trained in the Jungian tradition, sets out to state plainly the assumptions that underlie psychotherapy: what mental health actually is, and what analysts are trying to do when they treat a patient. He rejects the idea that there is a single normal pattern of adjustment to which all patients should be brought, whether that pattern is social conformity, sexual maturity in the Freudian sense, or any other fixed template. Instead he argues that the goal of therapy, and of life, is self-realization: each person's task is to discover and live out the particular pattern of potentialities they were born with, rather than to be squeezed into someone else's mould.

The book traces this task through the life cycle, from infancy through childhood and adolescence to adulthood, showing how the developing personality moves from a state of unconscious wholeness in the infant, through the pains of separation and individuation, toward a conscious integration of the different, often conflicting, sides of the self. Storr draws on his psychoanalytic and Jungian training but is deliberately eclectic, arguing that the particular school an analyst belongs to matters less than the quality of the analyst's attitude toward the patient. Along the way he discusses neurosis as a failure of this integrative process—a split within the personality in which parts of the self are disowned, repressed or projected outward rather than accepted and assimilated.

A recurring concern is the relationship between individuality and society. Storr insists that true integrity of personality often requires standing apart from convention, since the socially well-adapted person is not necessarily the psychologically healthy one; conformity can mask an impoverished or fragmented inner life. He examines the value of solitude and inner life as against an unreflective emphasis on relationships and adjustment to others, a theme he would return to at greater length decades later in Solitude. He also considers how apparently negative or destructive impulses—aggression, sexuality in its many forms, the shadow side of the self—need to be acknowledged and integrated rather than simply suppressed if a person is to become whole.

The book closes by returning to the therapeutic relationship itself, arguing that the analyst's role is not to impose values or engineer social adjustment but to help the patient recognize, tolerate and finally integrate the disparate elements of their own nature. Wholeness, for Storr, is not the elimination of conflict or darkness within the self but the achievement of a personality that can hold its contradictions together with honesty—hence the book's title, the integrity, in the sense of undividedness, of the personality.

ideas.title: Self-realization as the goal of life and therapy
ideas.summary: Storr argues that psychotherapy's real aim is not to make patients conform to any fixed social or sexual norm but to help them realize their own individual potential—to become what they most truly are. This reframes psychological health away from adjustment to society and toward authenticity to one's own nature.
ideas.evidence: He examines the assumptions underlying his own profession and proposes self-realization, rather than cure of symptoms or social adaptation, as the essential goal of the maturing person.

ideas.title: The relativity of personality
ideas.summary: There is no single template of the well-adjusted person; what counts as healthy or normal personality is relative to the individual's own constitution and life circumstances, not a universal standard. Storr uses this to challenge any therapeutic approach that measures patients against one ideal type.
ideas.evidence: This forms one of the book's early structural arguments, following directly from the opening discussion of self-realization.

ideas.title: Development from infancy to maturity
ideas.summary: Storr argues that becoming an integrated person is a developmental achievement, not a given: the infant starts in a state of unconscious wholeness, and growth necessarily brings separation, conflict, and the risk of splitting off unwanted parts of the self at each stage. Maturity means consciously reclaiming and integrating what earlier stages tended to disown, rather than simply outgrowing childhood.
ideas.evidence: He follows the individual's psychological history from childhood through adolescence to maturity, drawing on his clinical observation of patients at different life stages.

ideas.title: Neurosis as a split within the self
ideas.summary: Neurosis, for Storr, is not simply a set of symptoms but evidence of a personality divided against itself: parts of a person's nature are disowned, repressed, or projected onto others rather than accepted as one's own. Healing therefore means reintegrating what has been split off, not merely removing symptoms.
ideas.evidence: He discusses the causes of neuroses and other psychological problems as failures of integration rather than as isolated illnesses to be excised.

ideas.title: The analyst's attitude over the analyst's school
ideas.summary: Storr, trained as a Jungian, argues that what matters most in psychotherapy is not which theoretical school an analyst follows—Freudian, Jungian, or otherwise—but the quality of attentive, honest attitude the analyst brings to the patient. This is a synthesizing move that refuses sectarian rigidity in favor of the therapeutic relationship itself.
ideas.evidence: He states this directly, reflecting on his own Jungian training while insisting the analytic attitude toward the patient matters more than doctrine.

ideas.title: Integrity as undividedness, including one's dark side
ideas.summary: The book's title idea: psychological integrity means holding together, rather than eliminating, the contradictory and sometimes disreputable elements of one's nature—aggression, sexuality, ambition—so that the whole self is owned rather than partially disowned. Wholeness is not moral purity but honest self-acceptance of one's actual constitution.
ideas.evidence: Storr frames the goal of therapy and maturation as an integration of divergent impulses within the personality rather than their suppression.

ideas.title: The value of solitude and inner life against social conformity
ideas.summary: Storr resists the assumption, common in his profession and in popular thinking, that good relationships and social adjustment are the only or chief measures of mental health. He gives weight to the individual's inner, solitary life and self-discovery as equally vital to well-being—an idea he would expand decades later in Solitude.
ideas.evidence: This first book anticipates the argument later developed at length in Storr's Solitude, which draws on figures like Beethoven, Kant and Beatrix Potter to make the same case for solitary self-discovery.

key_claims_for_review.prompt: What does Storr propose as the true goal of psychotherapy, in place of curing symptoms or achieving social adjustment?
key_claims_for_review.answer: Self-realization: helping the patient discover and live out their own individual potential, rather than conforming to any fixed external standard of normality.

key_claims_for_review.prompt: How does Storr define neurosis in this book?
key_claims_for_review.answer: As a split within the personality, where parts of the self are disowned, repressed, or projected outward instead of being accepted and integrated.

key_claims_for_review.prompt: According to Storr, what matters more in psychotherapy than the theoretical school (Freudian, Jungian, etc.) an analyst belongs to?
key_claims_for_review.answer: The analyst's attitude toward the patient—an attentive, honest, non-doctrinaire relationship matters more than adherence to any particular theory.

key_claims_for_review.prompt: What does 'the integrity of the personality' mean as Storr uses the term?
key_claims_for_review.answer: Undividedness: the capacity to acknowledge and hold together all parts of one's nature, including aggressive or otherwise disreputable impulses, rather than achieving moral purity or suppressing them.

key_claims_for_review.prompt: Why does personality development, as Storr traces it from infancy onward, tend to produce splits within the self?
key_claims_for_review.answer: Because growth requires separation and the negotiation of conflict at each stage, and parts of the self that feel unacceptable or dangerous are apt to be disowned or repressed rather than integrated, unless maturity brings them back into conscious wholeness.

key_claims_for_review.prompt: What later, better-known book by Storr develops a theme first raised in The Integrity of the Personality?
key_claims_for_review.answer: Solitude: A Return to the Self, which expands his argument that inner, solitary self-discovery is as important to well-being as relationships with others.

key_claims_for_review.prompt: What is the 'relativity of personality', one of the book's early arguments?
key_claims_for_review.answer: The idea that there is no single universal template of the healthy or normal personality—what counts as psychological health is relative to each individual's own constitution and circumstances.
